articles.headline: With Kyler Murray back, will Vikings open up passing attack?
articles.description: Coach Kevin O'Connell said he is "still a believer in explosives" despite a long stretch of tepid air production for Minnesota.
articles.body:
EAGAN, Minn. -- Inside the visitors locker room Sunday at Soldier Field, Minnesota Vikings players peeled off layers of rain-soaked uniforms and equipment. Coach Kevin O'Connell soon launched into a postgame speech that precisely depicted his mindset, excitement -- and maybe even a bit of distress after a 9-3 victory over the Chicago Bears.

O'Connell praised players for "trying to figure out a way to find a way."

Later, he roared: "The only thing that matters is winning!"

That line represented the culmination of a very public reckoning O'Connell has put himself through while heading into his fifth season in Minnesota. The Vikings (2-0) have won seven consecutive games, dating back to last season, in ways that are almost unrecognizable from the pass-happy teams he first fielded upon arrival in 2022. But as quarterback Kyler Murray returns to the field, and with a hot but otherwise clear weather forecast Sunday at the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (4:05 p.m. ET, Fox), O'Connell has far from given up on the passing game he craves. 

"I'm still a believer in explosives," he said Monday. "I'm still a believer in taking some yards when they present themselves and doing it at a level where we pitch and catch at a level that I know our guys are capable of."

From 2022 to 2024, the Vikings put up the NFL's third-most passing yards (12,886) with the league's fifth-lowest rate of designed running plays (35.3%). They built their offense around receiver Justin Jefferson, who averaged a league-best 100.4 receiving yards per game over that period. Since that point, however, the Vikings rank No. 31 in passing yards (3,093) and have the league's fifth-fewest number of offensive plays -- rushing or passing -- that have gone for 10 yards or more (197). They've had fewer than 200 passing yards in 16 of their past 21 games.

Fortunately for them, that stretch has coincided with a defense and special teams that have been among the NFL's best, ranking No. 3 and 7 in expected points added (EPA), respectively. 

During their unbeaten start this season, with Murray playing only 11 snaps because of a concussion and leading rusher Jordan Mason going on injured reserve with a thumb injury after one week, the Vikings have managed a league-low 13 plays of 10 or more yards. O'Connell has protected the offense, particularly last week in Chicago, by leaning on the run game more than all but one other NFL playcaller. His rate of designed runs (50%) is higher than every team but the Seattle Seahawks, who also lost their starting quarterback (Sam Darnold) early in Week 1. Relatedly, the Vikings are tied with the Seahawks and Cincinnati Bengals for the NFL's fewest turnovers this season (one). 

"You've got to learn some things on how you approach trying to win one game every Sunday," O'Connell said this summer. "And they're all different. Every weekend is a challenge schematically, personnel-wise, where your team's at from a health standpoint, where your team's at with certain positions.

articles.headline: Denver Broncos to face another MVP QB in Matthew Stafford
articles.description: Sunday marks the 10th time the Broncos have faced an MVP quarterback since Vance Joseph became defensive coordinator in 2023. Can Denver get the best of Stafford?
articles.body:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- In weeks when the Denver Broncos are pitted against one of the NFL's best quarterbacks, defensive coordinator Vance Joseph often responds with a sigh when asked questions about how to stop them.

"That's our league, you know?" Joseph said. "Every week, every season, every time I look up I kind of feel like there is a quarterback waiting who can just punish you. Every week, man."

This is one of those weeks, as the Broncos will host the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday night at Empower Field at Mile High (8:20 p.m. ET, NBC). Reigning MVP Matthew Stafford will stand across from Joseph's defense six days after his 69th career 300-yard passing game and his 22nd career game with at least four touchdown passes.

He is also the last remaining active player who has been an NFL MVP that Joseph will face since being hired as Denver's defensive coordinator in 2023. The Broncos have played against Patrick Mahomes, Lamar Jackson, Aaron Rodgers and Josh Allen at least once since, and Sunday's match-up against Stafford and the Rams will complete the set.

The five quarterbacks have won a combined 10 MVP awards, including the last eight. They've had 10 meetings (including playoffs) against the Broncos over the past three-plus seasons. Denver has already faced one former MVP this season, losing to Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs 31-10 in the season opener. The loss to Mahomes makes those former MVPs 5-5 against the Broncos since Joseph became defensive coordinator.

The Broncos have allowed one 300-yard passing game in that stretch -- Mahomes threw for 306 yards in Week 6 of the 2023 season. They have thrown a combined 14 touchdown passes to nine interceptions and have been sacked 27 times (2.7 per game). Jackson had the best all-around day from that batch, completing 16 of 19 passes for 280 yards and three touchdowns in the Ravens' 41-10 win over the Broncos in Week 9 of the 2024 season. Allen had 283 passing yards and three touchdowns with two interceptions in the Broncos' overtime divisional round win this past January.

"Every week is a tough week because everybody has players who can make plays," Broncos cornerback Pat Surtain II said. "... But those quarterbacks at the top of their games, they force you to pay attention to all the details because the smallest things, the little details, that's all they need to put you in a bad spot. And once they find a bad spot, they're not going away from it until you take care of it."

The Broncos' defense re-calibrated from their Week 1 loss to the Chiefs with a Week 2 win over Jacksonville. The Broncos improved from giving up 173 rushing yards to Kenneth Walker III and missing an alarming 19 tackles against Kansas City to allow only 115 net yards and three points to the Jaguars in the second half to spark a comeback win. The Jaguars had 64 combined yards in their final three possessions of the game, which included an interception by Broncos cornerback Riley Moss.

articles.headline: Panthers' Bryce Young to Darren Waller has been money in red zone
articles.description: The veteran tight end's height, catch radius and history of red zone success make him a tough cover in big moments.
articles.body:
The connection between quarterback Bryce Young and tight end Darren Waller has been automatic for the Carolina Panthers in the red zone during the first two games of the 2026 regular season. And as the Panthers continue to put up points (they've scored 71!), Waller is at the heart of their red zone plans.

The veteran (6-foot-6 and 238 pounds) has towered over opposing defensive backs, particularly in the end zone. While he had a Week 1 touchdown catch called back for a questionable offensive pass interference penalty against the Chicago Bears, Waller snagged both of his Week 2 red zone targets from Young for two touchdowns against the Atlanta Falcons.

"Big people win," former Panthers QB Jake Delhomme, who now serves as a color commentator for the team's radio broadcasts, told ESPN. "Big people -- there's not many walking around this earth, right? Like [defensive end] Derrick Brown, there's not many walking around the earth like that. And when you have them, they help. ... The same thing with Waller, and [Falcons cornerback] C.J. Henderson [listed as 6-1] is not a small guy, and he made him look like he was like 5-9 on the touchdown in the corner right before half."

Waller, who signed a one-year deal with the Panthers in August, skipped the bulk of training camp and the entirety of the preseason as he got up to speed with Carolina's playbook. But since hitting the field for his Week 1 debut, the 34-year-old has hauled in all five of his targets for 61 yards and the two TDs. He has provided the Panthers with scoring opportunities they might not have had otherwise, and that has made him an intriguing option both in reality and in fantasy football.

Since coming out of retirement to play in nine games for the Miami Dolphins last season, Waller has run 37 routes in the red zone for Miami and Carolina in 11 total games. He has caught eight of his nine targets in the red zone for 62 yards and eight touchdowns. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Waller has 3.8 receptions over expected in the red zone (a stat that measures the difficulty against the completion probability for each catch), which is second only to San Francisco 49ers tight end George Kittle (5.3) from the start of the 2025 season through the first two games of 2026.

"I feel like, last year with Miami, getting there kind of late -- I got there earlier than I got here -- but just kind of dealing with trying to learn things quickly and try get in the mix, I feel like kind of gave me a little bit of a trial run of how to approach things and be as efficient as possible as far as learning and getting on the same page with the quarterback and things like that," Waller said in an interview with ESPN's "Unsportsmanlike" on Wednesday.

"So, I'm not really that surprised [by the early success in Carolina]. I feel like if I get some opportunities, I'm just going to try to make a play and keep it simple like that."

articles.headline: Meet Cam Achord: The Packers' secret special teams weapon
articles.description: Part old-school coach, part Gen Z analytics savant, Achord is "just a ball of energy" as he aims to fix Green Bay's special teams unit.
articles.body:
GREEN BAY, Wis. -- He wears cleats to practice even though he won't take a snap. He runs stride for stride with the kick returners, yet he doesn't have a ball in his hands. He takes a knee to demonstrate how kickers want the ball angled, but he's not a holder. He'll even throw himself -- nose first -- into a player even though he's not in pads.

He's Cam Achord, and he's here to change everything you ever thought about the Green Bay Packers' special teams.

The 39-year-old Mississippian is part your father's football coach with a hands-on, foul-mouthed approach, and part Gen Z analytics savant.

"He's one of a kind, there's no doubt about that," former New England Patriots special teams star Matthew Slater, who played for Achord from 2018 to 2023, told ESPN. "When you said that he's still running around out there with cleats on, I couldn't help but laugh to myself."

Not because Slater finds Achord funny. More a shake of the head because he still can't believe some of the things Achord does on the field.

"He wanted to make sure that we were prepared, even if that meant putting his body on the line," said Slater, a five-time All-Pro selection as a special-teamer. "I've seen Cam break a nose. I've seen him on the ground several times, but it's all in the name of ensuring that his players are ready to go. As a player, as a pro, you really have to appreciate that."

THE BROKEN NOSE story was largely unknown outside of the Patriots' inner circle before coach Matt LaFleur hired Achord in late February to replace Rich Bisaccia unexpectedly resigned.

It happened in 2019, when Achord was a Patriots assistant special teams coach. One day in practice, Achord was putting Justin Bethel, Slater and the other gunners through a drill designed to help them beat a double team, otherwise known as a vice.

"I tell them, 'Quit pulling me like you're gonna pull a coach,'" Achord recalled earlier this year. "I was like, 'Pull me like you're gonna pull the freaking vice. Yank!'"

And yank they did.

"Ask Justin about the broken nose," Slater said. "See if he remembers that."

Said Bethel: "Was it me?"

According to both Achord and Slater, yes, it was.

Bethel did exactly what Achord said, and the next thing anyone knew the coach was face down on the turf.

"So after that, I started wearing cleats just for better grip," Achord said.

Those cleats helped Achord in an August training camp practice, when he was nearly able to keep up with Bo Melton on a long kick return.

"He told me right before that play. He said, 'I'm running with your ass,'" Melton said. "So I was like, 'Oh man!'

"He brings it every day. Like whatever you do, he going to get on your ass when you do great. He's going to be happy as hell. He's going to be jumping around when you do good. And he going to rip your ass when you're not doing so well. So he's a through-and-through coach."

articles.headline: Baltimore Ravens feel prepared for Rio 'business trip'
articles.description: This is the Ravens' first game in Brazil, but coach Jesse Minter was there last season.
articles.body:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- A few days before playing the Dallas Cowboys, Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson was reminded that he is facing a franchise historically known as "America's Team."

"Yes, but this is America," Jackson said with a smile. "That is Brazil."

Jackson and the Ravens were in good spirits on Wednesday heading into one of their most challenging road trips in team history. Baltimore (1-1) will take a 10-hour flight to play the Dallas Cowboys (1-1) on Sunday in the NFL's first game in Rio de Janeiro (4:25 p.m. ET, CBS).

While there's been a lot of talk about the field condition at Maracanã Stadium, the Ravens believe there is a bigger factor for success in Brazil.

"I feel like the rhetoric around the game after it is done is who handled the travel and everything better," Ravens safety Kyle Hamilton said. "I think that just goes hand in hand on who is being more of a pro or not. That is something that I think we can thrive at."

This is the Ravens' first game in Brazil, but coach Jesse Minter was there last season. He was the defensive coordinator for the Los Angeles Chargers, who beat the Kansas City Chiefs, 27-21, in Sao Paulo.

Minter feels the biggest challenge is figuring out when to fly. The Ravens decided to stick to their normal practice on Wednesday and Thursday in Baltimore before leaving for Rio on a red-eye flight Thursday night.

The team will arrive in Brazil on Friday morning and will hold one full practice in the afternoon in Botafogo, which is about a half hour outside of Rio. The Ravens will get their first chance to see Maracanã Stadium on Saturday, when they will have a walkthrough there.

Minter chose not to leave earlier because it's only a one-hour time difference.

"I do not think there is a perfect answer for any of that stuff," Minter said. "It is all about how the team plays when the ball is kicked off."

Minter is already resigned to not sleeping much on the flight. But he acknowledged he doesn't sleep much on Thursday nights during the season anyway.

For the players, many will pass time by watching their favorite TV series.

"I just started watching Peaky Blinders, so [I'll] probably do a good bit of that, [and] sleep," Hamilton said of the British gangster show.

Wide receiver Rashod Bateman just started watching The Sopranos.

"They have a lot of episodes," Bateman said. "So I will try to catch up on that."

Jackson is thinking he will split up the time on the plane.

"I am just going to try to sleep as much as possible and just relax -- that is all I can do," Jackson said. "Keep my legs [moving and] try to walk around as much as possible, but at the same time sleep as much as possible. Five [hours awake] and five [hours sleeping] -- try to balance it out."

articles.headline: Orioles sweep doubleheader against Blue Jays to stave off elimination -- for now
articles.description: — Trey Gibson pitched brilliantly into the seventh inning and the Baltimore Orioles beat the Toronto Blue Jays 4-2 on Wednesday night to sweep a doubleheader and at least temporarily stay alive in the American League playoff race.
articles.body:
BALTIMORE -- — Trey Gibson pitched brilliantly into the seventh inning and the Baltimore Orioles beat the Toronto Blue Jays 4-2 on Wednesday night to sweep a doubleheader and at least temporarily stay alive in the American League playoff race.


              One more loss by the Orioles — or a win by the Chicago White Sox, who lost 5-4 at Kansas City on Wednesday night — would eliminate Baltimore. The Orioles also won the opener 4-2 against Toronto, then the 24-year-old Gibson (2-3) was outstanding in the nightcap.


              He would have completed at least seven innings if not for a rare defensive positioning violation that kept the top of the seventh going. Sean Keys grounded out to second for the third out, players left the field, and the Orioles were already playing “Thank God I'm a Country Boy” — which comes after "Take Me Out to the Ball Game" during the seventh-inning stretch — when an umpire interrupted the song to say the Blue Jays were challenging.


              A replay appeared to show second baseman Jeremiah Jackson's heel on the outfield grass before the grounder, so Keys was awarded first. The play was scored an error on Jackson, but no at-bat was charged to Keys. Gibson walked the next hitter and was pulled. Yennier Cano then issued a walk before striking out Myles Straw with the bases loaded to end the inning for real.


              In his eighth career start, Gibson allowed three hits in 6 2/3 scoreless innings with seven strikeouts and two walks. Christian Encarnacion-Strand homered and drove in three runs.


              Davis Schneider hit a two-run homer for Toronto in the ninth. The Blue Jays, eliminated from the playoff chase with their loss in the first game, are assured a losing season one year after winning the AL pennant.


              Toronto starter CJ Van Eyk (0-2) allowed four runs and four hits in five innings.


              Encarnacion-Strand opened the scoring with a two-run single in the first, then scored on Colton Cowser's double. Encarnacion-Strand's solo shot in the fourth made it 4-0.


              Two of the three hits Gibson allowed were infield singles in the third.


              Up next
              Both teams are off Thursday. The Orioles play the Yankees in New York on Friday night, and the Blue Jays host Cincinnati.


              ------

articles.headline: Alonso hits 41st homer as Orioles beat Blue Jays 4-2 to eliminate Toronto from the playoff race
articles.description: — Pete Alonso hit his 41st home run of the season, Chris Bassitt took a shutout into the sixth inning and the Baltimore Orioles beat the Toronto Blue Jays 4-2 in the first game of a doubleheader Wednesday, eliminating the defending American League...
articles.body:
BALTIMORE -- — Pete Alonso hit his 41st home run of the season, Chris Bassitt took a shutout into the sixth inning and the Baltimore Orioles beat the Toronto Blue Jays 4-2 in the first game of a doubleheader Wednesday, eliminating the defending American League champions from the postseason race.


              The Orioles and Blue Jays both entered this twin bill one loss from elimination. The best the Blue Jays (77-81) can do now is finish .500 — a season after they pushed the Los Angeles Dodgers to extra innings in Game 7 of the World Series.


              Max Scherzer (3-9) allowed four runs and four hits in five innings in the 500th appearance — and 491st start — of his career. He struck out seven and walked three. With his future uncertain, the 42-year-old right-hander could come back on short rest to pitch again Sunday in the season finale.


              The 37-year-old Bassitt (9-5) allowed two runs and seven hits in five-plus innings. He was pulled with two on in the sixth and both runners scored on second baseman Jeremiah Jackson's throwing error.


              Andrew Kittredge pitched the ninth for his 11th save.


              Scherzer struck out three in the first, but Jackson hit an RBI single in the second for the Orioles. With men on first and third and two out, Jackson took off for second, then stopped and got in a rundown. Colton Cowser was slow leaving third, but the Blue Jays kept going after Jackson, allowing Cowser to score.


              Alonso's two-run shot in the fifth pulled him even for the AL lead in homers with Houston's Yordan Alvarez and Tampa Bay's Junior Caminero. Alonso is eight RBI ahead of Alvarez for the league lead and may be the man who spoils the Houston slugger's pursuit of a Triple Crown.


              Up next
              Neither team had announced a starter for the second game Wednesday night.
